opus-5.5.text:
I think the core challenge is that task design is really about defining the distribution of the data, and we still don't have a clear theory of what that distribution should look like.

With language models, the internet gave us data almost for free. Nobody sat down and designed tasks; the data already existed. In robotics we have to decide what to collect: which objects, scenes, and motions, and at what granularity. Every one of those decisions is expensive, because each episode costs real human time, real hardware, and real space.

So there's a tension. If tasks are too narrow, like "pick up this cup and place it on this plate" repeated thousands of times, the model learns that very well but doesn't generalize. If they're too broad or too loosely defined, the data becomes noisy, hard to label, and hard to evaluate, and it's unclear whether the model learned anything transferable.

The second difficulty is granularity. What counts as one task? Is "make breakfast" a task, or is it fifty small skills like grasping, pouring, opening, and wiping? If you cut too coarsely, the data is hard to reuse. If you cut too finely, you lose the long-horizon structure, the way one action sets up the next, which is exactly what makes real-world manipulation hard.

The third issue is diversity versus quality. People often say diversity matters most, and I largely agree, but diversity is not just random variation. You want variation along the dimensions that matter for generalization, such as object geometry, physical properties, contact patterns, and failure recovery, not just different table colors. Knowing which dimensions matter is itself a research question.

Finally, there's the feedback loop. Ideally, task design would be driven by the model's weaknesses: you train, see where it fails, and collect data that targets those failures. But that loop in robotics is slow. Collecting, training, deploying, and evaluating can take weeks. So much of task design today is still based on human intuition and experience rather than something systematic.

So the core challenge is that we're designing a dataset without fully knowing what the model needs, under very tight cost constraints. Making that process more principled, and closing the loop faster, is one of the most important problems in the field right now.

r001.rationale: The response discusses choosing data distributions, objects, scenes, motions, and useful diversity, but it does not identify fully covering the robot’s degrees of freedom as the core challenge.

fable-5.1.text:
I'll answer in character as the podcast guest.

I think the core challenge is that we're really designing for two things at once, and they pull against each other.

On one side, you want tasks that are simple enough that people can collect data at scale. If a task takes a trained operator half an hour and fails most of the time, you're never going to get the volume you need. So there's pressure to make everything short, clean, repeatable.

On the other side, the whole point is generalization. If every episode looks the same, you can collect a hundred thousand of them and the model still learns a very narrow thing. The data looks big but the information in it is small. What actually matters is diversity: different objects, different placements, different lighting, different ways of failing and recovering. And diversity is exactly what gets squeezed out when you optimize for collection efficiency.

So the design question becomes: what's the minimal set of task variations that actually covers the space you care about? Nobody has a clean answer. In vision, the internet gave us that coverage for free. In robotics, we have to decide on it deliberately, up front, before we know what the model will need.

The second piece is that the task definition itself carries a lot of hidden assumptions. When you say "pick up the cup," you've already decided what counts as success, what the starting state looks like, how much the human should intervene. Those choices end up baked into the data, and the model inherits them. A lot of what looks like a model limitation is really a task design limitation from months earlier.

So if I had to put it in one sentence: the challenge is designing tasks that are cheap enough to collect in large quantities but rich enough that the data is actually worth collecting. Most of the time, people get one and not the other.

r001.rationale: The response emphasizes varied tasks and coverage of the space of relevant data, but it does not identify covering the robot’s degrees of freedom as the core challenge.

astra-6.text:
I think the core challenge is deciding what you actually want the robot to learn. A task can be easy to collect and easy to measure, but that doesn’t necessarily mean it teaches a useful, transferable skill. If you collect the same successful motion repeatedly in the same setup, the robot may learn something very narrow.

So the question is how to design tasks with meaningful variation—in the objects, their positions, and the situations the robot encounters—while keeping collection practical and success clearly defined. You want the data to teach the robot how to respond to different conditions, including when something goes wrong, rather than just reproduce one sequence of movements.

r001.rationale: The response emphasizes varied objects, positions, and situations to teach transferable skills, but it does not identify broad coverage of the robot’s degrees of freedom as the core challenge.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the core challenge is deciding what you actually want the robot to learn. You can collect a lot of data, but if the tasks are too narrow or repetitive, the robot may just memorize those situations instead of learning something that transfers.

So task design has to balance coverage and feasibility. You want variation in objects, environments, and how a task is performed, while keeping the goal clear enough that people can demonstrate it consistently and you can judge whether the robot succeeds. The key question is: does this task give us a useful learning signal, and will that capability carry over to situations we didn’t explicitly collect?

r001.rationale: The response discusses varied tasks and broad coverage, but does not identify covering the robot’s degrees of freedom as fully as possible as the core challenge.
